source.title: Clostridioides difficile-induced diarrhoea following dasatinib therapy

mappings.canonical_statement: The authors report a case of Clostridioides difficile infection arising during dasatinib therapy and frame it as a possible dasatinib-associated complication.
The patient was a 36-year-old Indian man with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia in accelerated phase.
Dasatinib therapy was started at 140 mg/day in September 2016.
After about 2 months of dasatinib therapy, the patient developed severe persistent diarrhoea with 20-25 bowel movements per 24 hours and crampy abdominal pain.
In the 2 months before gastrointestinal symptom onset, the patient reported no antibiotic or corticosteroid use and no medication other than dasatinib.
At presentation the patient was dehydrated and tachycardic, with pulse 108/min and blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, without fever or abdominal tenderness.
The article prints the white blood cell count as -6.85×10^9/L.
C-reactive protein was reported as 25 mg/L, with a stated reference value below 10 mg/L.
Liver function tests, renal function tests and electrolytes were reported within reference range.
Sigmoidoscopy showed confluent erythema, ulceration and pseudomembrane formation involving the sigmoid colon and rectum.

Histology showed focal crypt architectural disruption, mixed lamina propria inflammation with increased neutrophils, fibrin accumulation and cryptitis, with no leukaemic infiltration, dysplasia or organism identified.
Stool enzyme immunoassays were positive for C. difficile toxins A and B.
The authors diagnosed C. difficile infection on the basis of the clinical, endoscopic and toxin-assay findings.
The differential diagnosis included common enteric pathogens, opportunistic infections including CMV, neutropenic enterocolitis and CDI despite the absence of prolonged antibiotic exposure.
After CDI diagnosis, oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily was started and other medications were discontinued.
Supportive management included oral rehydration solution and probiotics, with routine monitoring of serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes.
Two weeks after metronidazole was started, diarrhoea subsided, stool consistency normalized and the patient made an uneventful recovery.
Repeat sigmoidoscopy after 14 days showed resolution of ulceration with normal-looking colonic mucosa.
Metronidazole therapy was continued for 3 weeks.
Dasatinib was restarted about 1 month after it had been stopped.
No recurrence of diarrhoea was reported during the next 2 years after dasatinib was restarted.
The authors highlight CDI as a possible complication of dasatinib therapy.
The authors hypothesize that dasatinib could predispose to CDI through kinase inhibition and effects on NK cells, T-regulatory cells and local intestinal immunity.
The learning points advise maintaining a high index of suspicion for C. difficile-induced diarrhoea in patients receiving chemotherapeutic drugs such as oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
The authors declared no specific grant from public, commercial or not-for-profit funding agencies.
The authors declared no competing interests.
Patient consent for publication was obtained.
The report states that it was not commissioned and was externally peer-reviewed.
